title: Choose the palette
scenario: A bakery asks for a header image for its winter menu. The brief is warm, cosy and appetising — but the last attempt came back in cool blue-grey tones that felt clinical and cold.
task: Which prompt gives the model the clearest direction toward a warm, appetising palette?

options.text: A bakery counter on a winter morning, beautiful warm and cosy colours, delicious pastries.
options.feedback: Feelings and praise again — nothing names an actual hue, so the model is free to return the cool look you just rejected.

options.text: A bakery counter in amber and cream with one deep-red accent, muted wood tones throughout, soft warm light.
options.feedback: Concrete hues, a dominant family, a support, one accent and a saturation level — every word is a decision the renderer can fulfil.

options.text: A bakery counter with maximum colour saturation and rainbow tones.
options.feedback: Saturation is a dial and this one is turned to maximum — loud is a different register from warm, and it walks away from the cosy brief.

options.text: A dark bakery counter in black and chrome, moody and minimal.
options.feedback: Muted, yes — but cool and dark reads austere. Cosiness needs warmth, not just restraint.

hints: Name hues the way paint shops do — amber, cream, rust — not the feeling you hope for.
Compare the temperature: which option actually commits to warm?
explanation: “Warm and cosy” is the goal; amber, cream and muted wood are the instructions that achieve it. A palette brief works when it names a dominant family (amber), a support (cream and wood), an accent (deep red) and a saturation level (muted). Each of those is renderable, and each is a dial you can turn — swap the accent and the mood changes without rebuilding the scene.
